# Recombination multisets — base ⟨2,2,3⟩ — dominance frontier

*Generated by `GenerateBaseMultisetFrontier --base=2x2x3 --bound=2`. Do not edit by hand.*

Base scheme: `2x2x3-r11-alphatensor_Z-682e003.json` (⟨2,2,3⟩ r=11, integer factors, Q).

> **The frontier is specific to this GL-representative.** `enumerate` sweeps the
> `GL×GL×GL` isotropy orbit only — *not* the transpose/duality symmetries that make all
> rank-`r` schemes of a shape equivalent. So a different rank-`r` base of the same shape can
> yield a different multiset variety and a different frontier (e.g. Strassen ⟨2,2,2⟩ → 8,
> Winograd/AlphaTensor-Z ⟨2,2,2⟩ → 7). Re-run with the base you intend to recombine.

## Why a frontier (not the full set)

A recombination sends each of the base's `r` products to a sub-matmul whose per-axis size is the
block it lands on (**index 0 = largest block = most expensive**, under *any* allocation). The total
rank is `Σ R(sub-shapeₖ)`, and matmul rank is **monotone** (a bigger sub-multiply never costs less —
pad the small one in). So if multiset *A* matches *B* product-by-product with every *A*-block ≤ the
paired *B*-block, then `cost(A) ≤ cost(B)` for **every** base recursion, and *B* can never be optimal.
Keeping only the **dominance frontier** (the non-dominated antichain) is therefore *lossless for the
rank minimum* and *allocation/base-independent*. The frontier is an antichain — it cannot collapse to
one point because the three axes are coupled (a product is one corner-type across all axes at once),
so several incomparable trade-offs survive; the minimum at any concrete allocation is one of them.

## Summary

Two quotient levels. **Canonical** = multisets up to the base's axis symmetry (the right level for symmetric / axis-permuted allocations; dominance is axis-permutation aware). **Axis-tagged** = no quotient (lossless for asymmetric allocations too, where axis identity matters). Both frontiers are seed-independent.

## Canonical frontier multisets

Symbolic in the block sizes (`x₁` = largest part of axis x, `x₂` next, …). Sorted by total
"smallness" (cheapest sub-shape mass first). `pure-big` = products on the all-largest block;
`pure-small` = products on the all-smallest block; `mixed` = the rest.
